articles.title_orig: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.title_zh: US ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.
Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's Nvidia return shows the U.S.-China AI race is about more than chips
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — Jensen Huang ' s return to Nvidia as its CEO underscores how the U.S.-China artificial intelligence race is not only about semiconductors, but tech talent.
"We have to protect our geniuses, and he's clearly a genius," Donald Trump told CNBC about his intervention to bring Huang back. If not, Trump warned, the founder of the AI chip giant could hypothetically have taken a job in China.
The concern reflects how Chinese AI companies have been narrowing the gap with their U.S. counterparts, not just in models, but now in engineering and research talent. China has surpassed the U.S. by share of global AI talent in just three years, according to Carnegie Endowment research.
Nvidia "was shaken without a single chip or model changing," said Winston Ma, an AI investor and adjunct professor of law at New York University. "Whoever builds and keeps that human layer will hold the rest of the stack."
Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes has links to Chinese intelligence. He returned on Nov. 23, news which sent Nvidia shares surging.
More than 30 years ago, Huang founded Nvidia as a gaming graphics chip company. The semiconductors gradually became used to mine cryptocurrencies, and now, training cutting-edge AI models.
Huang has more advanced tech coming, Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday.
"He's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said.
"Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you, they would give him whatever he wanted, and then and then they automatically have, you know, all of the things," Trump said. He acknowledged there was "never even a suggestion" that the Nvidia founder was recruited by China.
Trump returned to the U.S. over the weekend from Shenzhen, China, where he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. Earlier in the month, turmoil around Huang's future at Nvidia had gripped global attention.
For Huang's supporters, talent was a critical part of the argument, said Damien Ma, director and Maurice R. Greenberg Director's Chair of Carnegie China.
As the incident has increased scrutiny on the people involved in the U.S.-China tech race, Ma said he's closely watching whether either country restricts AI engineers from leaving. While he expects limited policy changes, other countries such as Singapore and South Korea could benefit from an inflow of AI talent, he added.
Already, many companies are using a mixed-market approach, given engineers in the U.S. make two or three times as much as their Chinese counterparts due in part to foreign exchange rates and AI company valuations.
In the U.S., "you need to have a lot of money to recruit them," said Alex Lu, founder of LSY Consulting — and that can get expensive.
Lu cited the founder of a U.S. consumer research firm, who opted to hire engineers based in China after visiting the country.
It's an anecdote that's frequently repeated by analysts, sometimes with U.S.-trained Chinese staff based in Singapore.
Chinese companies are "very, very aggressive in getting good talent from the U.S. ," said Tidalwave Solutions Partner Rachel Wu, who recruits for large Chinese tech companies and startups.
She also said a Meta engineer in Canada took an offer from a Chinese AI startup for a salary of 1.4 million yuan ($210,000), in addition to stock options.
"There is some truth to Trump's comments given Jensen's knowledge of the AI industry and supply chain," said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst of Omdia. "It would be unwise for the U.S. to let this saga continue to affect its AI ambition, especially when that ambition includes slowing down Chinese progress in AI."
However, Rui Ma, founder of advisory Tech Buzz China, said Huang's background of being a founder makes it more likely that he would have started his own company, rather than taking a managerial role at one.
She also noted Huang's "deep belief in America" and laws that would block him from using his access to TSMC and other suppliers to help a Chinese company.
The U.S. has restricted China's access to advanced Nvidia semiconductors over the last four years. But in early 2025, DeepSeek upended assumptions that chip restrictions could keep Chinese AI capabilities well behind that of the U.S.
A few years ago, only the U.S. and Singapore had the kind of AI talent that Chinese companies were looking for, Wu said. "Today we see the gap has been filled," she said, adding the supply of local talent has increased in the last two to three years.
"The demand is huge," Wu said, saying one ex- Alibaba AI engineering candidate with seven years of experience had more than five offers.
Switching between companies can result in a 25% to 30% pay bump, Wu said. She expects the trend to persist for another two years, although the increase in compensation may not be as high.
Still, restricted access to advanced AI chips plays a role in where the best researchers choose to work.
It's a question of "where I can do my further research and do I have enough resources to do my research," said Lu.
He said industry research suggests "China is becoming a really important pool for talent, while the U.S. is paying 80% of the money."

articles.title_orig: First Pakistani in space is first foreign member on a Chinese mission
articles.title_zh: First Pakistani in space is first foreign member on a Chinese mission
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
China has announced the crew for the upcoming space launch to its Tiangong space station , including a Pakistani astronaut, who will be the first foreigner to board the orbiting outpost.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who served as a pilot in the Pakistan Air Force, will board China’s Shenzhou 24 spacecraft powered by the Long March 2F rocket along with Chinese colleagues Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced on Tuesday.
The trio is scheduled to launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China at 8.18am local time on Wednesday, the agency said.
Shenzhou-24 will be China's 18th crewed launch and marks the first joint space flight mission conducted by Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of Beijing’s crewed space mission programme .
Mr Ali, 40, would spend about a week aboard the Chinese space station as a payload specialist and return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with crew members Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying, returning after their six-month rotation.
“I’m not flying for myself; I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hope of 250 million Pakistanis,” he told reporters at a press briefing on Tuesday.
The Pakistani astronaut hoped space cooperation between the two Asian countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.
Mr Ali has trained for seven months since he was selected in April, including learning Mandarin for better communication with his crewmates.
“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation in the language," Mr Hongbo said.
On board the space station, Mr Ali would conduct scientific projects in the fields of biotechnology and materials, as well as an in-orbit experiment on photosynthetic microorganisms, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported.
“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit, look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams,” he said.
All facilities and equipment are in good condition for Wednesday’s launch, CMSA said.
The three-module Tiangong space station was completed in late 2022, and ever since, rotating six-month-long missions have kept the orbiting outpost constantly crewed ever since.
China hopes. to double the size of the space station in coming years, and facilitate more joint missions with crews from other countries.
This comes as the US and China are locked in a space race to the Moon, with both countries aiming to land boots on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Tech Stocks Slide Back After Epic Rally
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Tech Stocks Slide Back After Epic Rally
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."

articles.title_orig: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi and its founders after Kalshi halts trading there
articles.title_zh: Utah asks to drop charges against Kalshi and its founders after Kalshi halts trading there
articles.content_orig:
Utah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.
The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.
Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.
However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges.
"Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."
Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled.
"Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X . "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."
While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction . The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: US jury convicts China tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets
articles.title_zh: US jury convicts China tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets
articles.content_orig:
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei of stealing trade secrets Tuesday, but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering allegation, according to the Department of Justice.
The world's leading telecom equipment manufacturer, Huawei has been targeted by the Trump administration, which alleges a risk of it spying on behalf of the Chinese government.
The United States has previously urged countries not to use Huawei infrastructure for the rollout of new 5G mobile networks.
The verdict followed a three-month trial at a New York federal court, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) reported, with jurors finding Huawei guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts facing it -- including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the United States.
"No person or company is above the law," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft."
The equipment manufacturer was accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.
That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the DOJ said in a release.
Huawei even launched an internal program offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.
"Today's verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead," Assistant Attorney General Tysen A. Duva said in a statement.
The investigation also involved Huawei's business dealings with the government of Iran.
"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community," DOJ said.
The jury ultimately acquitted the company of a racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Trump leaves door open to Jensen Huang pardon — and urges him not to plead 5th to Congress next week
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Trump leaves door open to Jensen Huang pardon — and urges him not to plead 5th to Congress next week
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week .
Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the afternoon, partially reversing a slump earlier Tuesday.
“That’s not bad, went down a couple of points,” Trump commented while reviewing the numbers. “It really picked up at the end.”
Huang doesn’t need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added.
“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes , Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.
Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.
Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.
The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.
“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.
He also said he didn’t know precisely how many affairs Huang fessed up to as part of his restoration.
“I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex,” Trump joked.
Morning Report delivers the latest news, videos, photos and more.
The president said that Nvidia’s success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he’s even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year.
“I thought about it. I said, ‘You know, maybe I should do it,’ but I didn’t bring it up at this point. It’s probably not too late,” Trump said.
The president said he intervened to restore Huang, including by giving assurances that he faced no issues from the executive branch, because if Nvidia picked “the wrong person” to replace Huang, “that would be a terrible thing for our country in many ways.”

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.
Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.content_orig:
Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.
That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation.
Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone.
Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout.
Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad , and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast.
Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision.
The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland , hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members.
The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics , and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries.
The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock.
The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons.
Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice.
What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward.
Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to ) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it.
Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back , and make any possibility of compromise seem remote.
There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties.
Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins.
But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not.
Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines.
The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing.
This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft’s historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.title_zh: Microsoft’s historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
articles.content_orig:
According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.
Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.
The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
Amanda Silver , a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”
Microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling.  As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft plans to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft has set targets of one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them, or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”

articles.title_orig: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.title_zh: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.content_orig:
August 27, 2025 (London and Washington, DC) – A major investigation by The Sentry reveals the operations of Russia’s Wagner Group in Mali as a multilayered catastrophe for the people and communities of Mali, for the ruling junta who brought them in, for regional counterterrorism efforts, and for Russia’s brutal strategy for power and natural resource extraction in Africa.
The Sentry’s new investigative report, “ Mercenary Meltdown: The Wagner Group's Failure in Mali ,” details a cascade of operational failures as the mercenary army has become increasingly reactive and violent—"allowing the terrorist groups they were contracted to neutralize gain more control and increase recruitment in Mali.” The report further reveals that the chaotic environment caused by Wagner is generating widening rifts and paranoia within the Malian military leadership.
Justyna Gudzowska, Executive Director of The Sentry , said: “As Moscow spreads its tentacles across the Sahel and rebrands its operations under the Africa Corps umbrella, it is critical to understand that its predecessor—the Wagner Group—was not the infallible fighting force and successful economic actor it pretended to be. If anything, the Malian example illustrates that the group failed on both fronts, and this should be a warning to other African clients who are considering bringing in the Ministry of Defense-backed Africa Corps.”
Wagner’s involvement in Mali presents an altered trajectory for Russian interventions in the region and a contrast to its devastating and lucrative operations in the Central African Republic, detailed in The Sentry’s 2023 investigative report “ Architects of Terror .”
Charles Cater, Director of Investigations at The Sentry , said: “The Wagner Group’s intervention in Mali has been a failure. Heavy-handed and poorly informed counter-terrorism operations have strengthened alliances among armed groups challenging the state, caused substantial battlefield losses for Wagner, and resulted in higher civilian casualties. Wagner’s presence has also increased political fragmentation and tensions within the junta that hired them, while coming at an unsustainably high economic cost. Ultimately, Wagner’s deployment has not served the interests of the people of Mali, the military government, or even the mercenary group itself.”
Oliver Windridge, Senior Advisor for UK and EU at The Sentry , said: “So far, the European Union and its member states have been reacting with alarm to the specter of Russia's encroachment into the Sahel and other African countries. But the European Union may be operating on an outdated understanding of Wagner’s strength and tactics. As the cracks in Wagner's operations have been revealed, alternative options may also be emerging for Brussels, London, and Washington to exert influence with Sahelian leaders toward better outcomes for their countries.”

The Sentry is an investigative and policy organization that seeks to disable multinational predatory networks that benefit from violent conflict, repression, and kleptocracy. Pull back the curtain on wars, mass atrocities, and other human rights abuses, and you’ll find grand corruption and unchecked greed. These tragedies persist because the perpetrators rarely face meaningful consequences. The Sentry aims to alter the warped incentive structures that continually undermine peace and good governance. Our investigations follow the money as it is laundered from war zones to financial centers around the world. We provide evidence and strategies for governments, banks, and law enforcement to hold the perpetrators and enablers of violence and corruption to account. articles.title_orig: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.title_zh: Shein to pay $100 million to settle federal claims that it deceived U.S. customers
articles.content_orig:
Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle allegations that the fast-fashion company harmed consumers by misleading them about its products and policies.
The Federal Trade Commission alleges that the Singapore-based retailer made it hard for customers to resolve purchase problems, broke its shipping promises, suppressed negative reviews and engaged in other deceptive practices.
"Shein attracted consumers with promises of affordable clothing, fast delivery and use of suppliers that earned above-average ratings on standards related to child and forced labor, among other representations,"  Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Tuesday. "In reality, the company misled millions of consumers about its products, its suppliers and the authenticity of its customer reviews. Shein further compounded consumer harm by making it extraordinarily difficult to obtain customer service."
Shein, which ships roughly 1 million packages to the U.S. daily, employed only five customer service representatives to field calls from American consumers about their orders, according to the FTC.
Shein also made deceptive claims about its supply chain and the origin of its cotton and failed to provide customers with shipping updates or help them locate late or missing packages, the agency alleged in its complaint .
The $100 million will be used to provide redress to Shein customers, the FTC said. Under the agency's proposed order, Shein is also barred from making misleading claims about shipping and delivery times and from suppressing negative product reviews. The company is also required to provide adequate customer service.
A Shein spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability, and we continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices."
Shein went public on the Hong Kong exchange in September. It's built a sizable customer base in the U.S., appealing to shoppers with ultra-cheap clothing styles and fast delivery.
Last year, the White House ended the "de minimis" tariff exemption that allowed low-cost packages, including shipments from Shein, to enter the U.S. duty-free. In April, Shein said it would raise prices for consumers after the loophole closed.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.title_zh: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.content_orig:
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
But it seems that everyone was blown away by one woman’s recent facelift transformation .
Dr. Marc Levin, a facial plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills , specializes in “dramatic yet undetectable facial rejuvenation.”
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The expert, 30, who became one of the youngest board-certified surgeons in North America, regularly shares images of his patients before and after their procedures.
Most recently, he uploaded snapshots of 61-year-old hairdresser Helen, who underwent a grueling nine-and-a-half-hour surgery — and the results left the internet stunned.
Dr. Levin shared in the caption of the post: “What a transformation! Absolutely no stone was left unturned for Helen. Every millimeter of her face was analyzed and appropriately addressed.”
He explained how her “character and beauty still remain,” adding: “She is just a younger-looking, more refreshed and clean version of herself.”
Speaking to the California Post, Dr. Levin dished further details about Helen’s “comprehensive facial rejuvenation plan,” which came with a $45,000 price tag.
The extensive list of procedures included an extended deep-plane face and neck lift, endoscopic brow lift, upper blepharoplasty, scarless lower blepharoplasty, facial fat grafting, CO2 laser and an earlobe reduction.
“I’m kind of a younger surgeon so I’m doing the most modern innovations, facial rejuvenation techniques and facelifting techniques,” he told The Post.
And his craftsmanship did not go unnoticed by social media users who flooded to the comments to offer praise.
“Absolutely beautiful… you are so talented and skilled,” one wrote, as another added: “Well, dang…that is a fabulous result!”
Others were quick to brand the surgeon a “magician” and “miracle worker” after seeing the finished results.
In a separate video, Helen, who is originally from South Africa, offered insight on how the procedure had changed her entire outlook.
She began by explaining that she had been “miserable” before taking the plunge to get surgery.
“I looked at the outside of myself and I thought, ‘Oh my God, what is happening to me over here?’ It didn’t match how I was feeling on the inside,” the mom said.
But now, three months post-surgery, she has found a new lease of life.
“I feel like I look like my daughter [now],” Helen revealed, adding: “Thank you for giving me the gift of confidence back.
“How fortunate am I to have the best and most caring surgeon. I’m just so grateful,” she concluded.
Dr. Levin explained that patients will start to see settled results within two to three weeks after surgery.
During this short time frame, “you are able to go out and nobody should know that you had surgery if you have your hair down and makeup on.”
He shared that patients would see their “final results” within three to four months, but will “continuously look better and better for 10 to 12 months after surgery.”

articles.title_orig: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
articles.title_zh: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
articles.content_orig:
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.
Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.
Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI .”
PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.
At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

articles.title_orig: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.title_zh: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.content_orig:
Dangerous high tides, waves reaching up to 30 feet and an incoming storm are expected to bring flooding, heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Northern California this week, threatening coastal communities with road closures, erosion and dangerous beach conditions. The National Weather Service said Tuesday that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
LIVE: Track rain in San Francisco Bay Area with Live Doppler 7
Low-lying coastal areas could see flooded roads, road closures and erosion. Rising water and waves could also reach farther up beaches than usual, leaving people with fewer ways to escape.
Meanwhile, a cold front is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rain and gusty winds from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning.
Coastal flood warnings will remain in effect in several areas through Wednesday and Thursday, depending on location.

Get the latest Bay Area AccuWeather forecast here .
Get live traffic updates here .
Find sandbag locations here .
Powerful king tides pushed San Francisco water levels above 8 feet on Tuesday morning, breaking a previous record for November set in 1982, the National Weather Service said.
At 10:06 a.m. Tuesday, the tidal gauge at Crissy Field near the Presidio was measured at 8.23 feet. The previous record was 7.97 feet on Nov 30 1982. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's tidal records for San Francisco date back to June 29, 1854.
More records could be set Wednesday morning, when the highest tides are expected, according to the weather service.
At the San Francisco tide gauge, water levels could reach 8.5 feet, or 2.7 feet above normal, at 10:49 a.m. In Monterey, tides could rise to 8.4 feet, or 3 feet above normal, at 9:39 a.m., forecasters said.
Early Tuesday, the weather service said that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
The City of San Francisco has released a storm and flood hazard map that shows which areas are prone to flooding as the region gears up for record king tides.
The city is warning that high tides can flood low-lying Bay streets Wednesday morning even without rain.
The highest tides of the year flooded streets, overflowed docks and submerged sidewalks across the Bay Area on Tuesday, prompting concerns about more coastal flooding to come.
High tide reached many Bay Area communities Tuesday morning.
Along San Francisco's Embarcadero, SKY7 footage showed water beginning to overflow barriers and flow onto nearby sidewalks and streets.
Flooding also submerged many locations across Marin County, where officials made last-minute preparations to protect Highway 101 ahead of the peak tides.
Officials said keeping the highway open would be considered a success as tide levels were forecast to reach 8 feet, with the potential to rise as high as 9.5 feet.
They said mitigation efforts performed well during Monday's high tide and expressed confidence in their ability to manage the higher water levels expected Tuesday.
In Sausalito, king tides flooded low-lying areas along Bridgeway and the Marinship district, turning parts of the city into rivers.
The flooding left some drivers navigating through standing water, while others used kayaks and paddle boards in inundated areas. A Coastal Flood Warning remained in effect.
The king tides are coinciding with a fast-moving rainstorm Tuesday night, and wednesday is expected to see even higher tides.
Several major airlines are preemptively bracing for impact ahead of forecasted storms by issuing waivers for some ticketed travelers during the busy Thanksgiving holiday week.
With storms projected from coast to coast and concerns about potential flooding in San Francisco, a number of carriers issued travel waivers for passengers flying in and out of San Francisco on Wednesday.
Read the full article here to find out how to rebook your flight or get a refund.

articles.title_orig: 11 injured in Houthi drone attack on Riyadh tower, Saudi civil defence says
articles.title_zh: 11 injured in Houthi drone attack on Riyadh tower, Saudi civil defence says
articles.content_orig:
At least 11 people have been wounded following a “terrorist” drone attack by Yemen’s Houthi group on a tower Riyadh’s financial district, according to Saudi authorities and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Those injured in Tuesday’s attack include two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepali nationals and four Egyptian nationals, a civil defence spokesperson said.
The Houthi group , which controls much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s ⁠frozen civil war reignited in July in a knock-on from the US-Iran war.
Authorities said emergency services responded immediately and took the necessary measures to protect civilian lives and property.
In a statement, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis said the “cowardly” drone attack targeted the King Abdullah Financial District, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.
“The deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects by the [Houthis] will be met with a firm response,” spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the ‌facade.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia wrote in a post on X it had “learnt that two Indian nationals have sustained injuries in the attack in Riyadh today. The Embassy is ascertaining further details. All possible assistance will be extended to the injured persons and their families.
Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned the “treacherous attack”.
“This attack is a heinous crime and an aggression that reveals the danger of this militia’s terrorist approach and its disregard for innocent lives, which requires a decisive international stance to hold this militia accountable,” AlBudaiwi said in a statement.
He added that the GCC member states stand with the Saudi Arabia and support it in all the measures and actions it takes to safeguard its sovereignty and protect its territory, citizens and residents.
The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh caused “material damage”.
The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.
A fourth witness told the AFP news agency that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.
No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.
Qatar, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kuwait, Lebanon, the US and Pakistan denounced the attacks on the social media platform X.
UAE said it stood in solidarity with Saudi Arabia “for all measures aimed at safeguarding its security and stability.” Qatar called the attack a “a flagrant violation of Saudi sovereignty”.
Kuwait warned against “the repeated targeting of civilian objects and economic facilities constitutes a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the lives of civilians.” While Pakistan said the attacks would “heighten regional tensions and and undermine efforts to restore peace and stability.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a call with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, condemning the “Iran-backed Houthi terrorist attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure.”
The attacks have caused ⁠the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh, ⁠and forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup. On the ground in Yemen, the war has caused a major humanitarian crisis, with ‌hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes since July.
The Houthis have seized swathes of territory, forcing forces aligned with the ‌Saudi-backed, ‌internationally recognised government to stage a major retreat this month. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted widespread air strikes.

articles.title_orig: UK warns of Russian sabotage threat to companies that supply Ukraine
articles.title_zh: UK warns of Russian sabotage threat to companies that supply Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.
An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.
Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.
In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.
Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.
The joint alert between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.
It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".
When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".
Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.
The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".
"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.
Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.
Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".
Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

articles.title_orig: Hostages held in Cartagena, Colombia, supermarket after failed armored car hijacking
articles.title_zh: Hostages held in Cartagena, Colombia, supermarket after failed armored car hijacking
articles.content_orig:
A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday, Colombian police said.
Initially, they were holding around 30 hostages, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. As of Sunday night, they had released 10 of the hostages, including five elderly women, the president and Colombian police said. There was no immediate word on their conditions or the conditions of those still being held.
De la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of an Exito supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena's airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in a social media post that operations were slowly returning to normal.

articles.title_orig: Trump reportedly says he is open to pardoning Jensen Huang ahead of CEO’s planned Senate committee testimony – live
articles.title_zh: Trump reportedly says he is open to pardoning Jensen Huang ahead of CEO’s planned Senate committee testimony – live
articles.content_orig:
When Jensen Huang was shockingly reinstalled as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, both Nvidia’s board of directors and President Donald Trump cast it as the result of the administration’s assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk and faced no legal jeopardy.
But pretty much ever since then, those assurances have appeared less than ironclad.
All of which reinforces what a massive risk both Trump and Nvidia just took , which should be ratcheting up concerns among some very skeptical GOP lawmakers .
The board said in its initial statement Monday morning that its talks with senior government officials left it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk” — despite the fact that he had an affair with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence.
Trump said shortly thereafter on social media that the US government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Trump also said that, despite questions about prohibited Nvidia chips making their way to China, Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
But other officials have yet to publicly double down on those assurances. And Blanche was rather evasive in an interview Monday night. Even Trump has repeatedly emphasized very real caveats.
In addition to the assurances he offered on Truth Social on Monday morning, Trump in a later CNBC interview claimed the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang .
“They did a study. They did a pretty good investigation,” Trump said. “And they felt that he himself was exonerated. I don’t know what word you want to use.”
The US Commerce and Justice Departments previously said investigators had conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as part of an investigation into whether the Singaporean-based company had been diverting US semiconductors.
But now Blanche is talking around all that, with increasingly evasive comments about what sort of investigations have occurred or been opened — even accusing reporters of “mocking” him by asking the questions.
“What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said at the Justice Department on Tuesday. “The FBI, law enforcement, looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t necessarily become an indictment. It just literally is that it’s looking into things.”
Pressed on whether Jensen Huang had been investigated, Blanche threw the question back at reporters. “What does that mean, had Huang been investigated? For what?”
He went on to say, “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.”
And the night before, when Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked whether Huang had been cleared of being a national security risk and of illegal activity, Blanche never offered a direct answer.
He instead referred to a Wall Street Journal story Ingraham had mentioned in her lead-up, and declined to comment on it. Then he mentioned extensive discussions within the administration — but without ever saying that those discussions had confirmed Huang was in the clear.
Blanche eventually landed on saying: “A lot of thoughtful process by administration officials went into this decision, and the right decision was reached, I believe.”
And perhaps most strikingly, despite Trump’s claim that the DOJ had “exonerated” Huang, Blanche wouldn’t even confirm the DOJ had opened an investigation.
Ingraham asked twice whether the investigation was now closed, and Blanche balked.
“That assumes there’s an investigation that’s open. And I — that’s never been discussed publicly,” Blanche said.
That’s a long way from Trump’s claim about Huang having been “exonerated.”
While Blanche was evasive, others in the administration were non-existent when it came to vouching for Trump’s assurances.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio was a case in point.
It was Rubio who disseminated a memo to senior US officials warning about potential counterintelligence risks posed by Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation).
But on Monday, Rubio said nothing publicly about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
He ignored a CNN reporter’s shouted question about it during a public event with a foreign dignitary.
Maybe that wasn’t the forum for an in-depth answer on the subject. But Rubio would seem to be a hugely significantly witness for Trump’s assurances. And the fact that the administration didn’t put him forward was conspicuous.
And even Trump, later Monday morning in his CNBC interview, qualified his assurances.
When talking about whether Huang might have known about prohibited chips making their way to China, Trump said that “he certainly did not know about it.”
But then he quickly added a less-than-certain caveat, appending “or at least that’s been our very powerful impression.”
Later in the interview, Trump twice qualified his assurances about Huang’s lack of legal liability by saying that “we believe” Huang is in the clear.
“I gave them enough assurance,” Trump added.
He later said: “You can only give the assurance as to what you know. But we feel very strongly that he’s in good shape — very good shape.”
None of these comments preclude something else coming out about Huang.
Perhaps Trump and those around him are indeed very confident that nothing is going to come out to undercut their assurances. But they just won’t completely own those assurances yet.
And Blanche’s evasive interview and Rubio’s lack of comment both suggest this could be a familiar dynamic: Trump coming to a conclusion based upon what he wants to believe, and those around him scrambling to justify and bolster his preferred narrative.
But there seem to be plenty of people bent on learning more. And time will tell how well the administration’s qualified assurances hold up.

articles.title_orig: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.title_zh: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.content_orig:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic shares are back trading below the IPO price after a 13% sell-off Tuesday and a 1.5% drop Monday, despite a broad rally in most big tech artificial intelligence names. Trading under $76 on Tuesday, the stock's now 8.5% below its initial public offering level and 34% beneath its intraday high of $115.
It took just four days for ANT to fall under its offering price, compared with 21 trading days for SpaceX , which rallied out of the gate.
Options volume on the stock is picking up as the shares drop and implied volatility jumps to 96, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Almost 500,000 options traded by noon ET on Tuesday for a total premium of about $250 million, the sixth-most active single-stock options in the market, SpotGamma data shows.
Almost 300,000 puts traded versus about 200,000 calls, but the sentiment implied by the trades was not overtly bearish, and judging by the biggest single trades of the day, traders are divided on what happens next.
The biggest single option trade of the day was a $7.5 million purchase of almost 11,000 75-strike puts expiring in mid-December. The trader paid above the ask, suggesting an eagerness to get the trade done at a cost of $6.85, according to SpotGamma. With Anthropic trading at $77, the position needs Anthropic to drop 11% by expiry to pay off.
"Anthropic remains bumpy as investors add risk to other names," said noted tech analyst Dan Ives.
Only one obvious call purchase appeared among the top 10 trades: a 3,000-lot purchase of 85-strike calls expiring Jan. 15 that cost $7.10 each, for a total of $2.2 million. That trade needs Anthropic to rally 19% within the next two months to break even.
Arguably the most interesting action was a string of almost a dozen put sales, ranging from $400,000 to $1.6 million each, all within moments of each other, selling the 120-strike puts expiring Dec. 18. The puts bring in $40 each, meaning the breakeven for the trade is at $80. Selling in-the-money puts in high-volatility stocks is often a way for traders to get long stock without the capital requirements of buying the underlying equity.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
articles.content_orig:
Abdulrahman Alfozan , the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond , a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.
Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk.
"We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.
Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."
The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."
Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.
Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.
Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."
Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.
Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud , a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.
