articles.title_orig: Lukashenko Offers to Fly Zelensky to Moscow as ‘Security Guarantor’
articles.title_zh: Lukashenko Offers to Fly Zelensky to Moscow as ‘Security Guarantor’
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko offered to fly to Moscow with President Volodymyr Zelensky for direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and act as his security guarantor. In an interview with French magazine Le Point recorded on Nov. 17 – due to be published in full on Wednesday, Nov. 25 – Lukashenko also argued that Ukraine, Belarus and Russia would agree on ending the war faster without European participation. Later on Tuesday, Zelensky countered that Lukashenko should bring Putin to Kyiv instead, promising both leaders a safe reception for negotiations.
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has offered to fly to Moscow together with President Volodymyr Zelensky for a direct meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, pledging to act as Zelensky’s security guarantor.
Zelensky dismissed the idea, countering that Lukashenko should instead bring Putin to Kyiv and promising both leaders a safe reception, RBC-Ukraine reported .
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Lukashenko made the proposal in an interview with the French news magazine Le Point, recorded on Nov. 17, according to the Belarusian presidential website . The full interview is expected to be published on Wednesday, Nov. 25, Belarusian state news agency BelTA reported.
“Volodymyr Zelensky and I could get on a plane and fly to Moscow. Just the two of us,” Lukashenko said, as quoted by Ukrainska Pravda . “I could get on a plane with him and fly to Moscow as his security guarantor,” he added.
The roughly 90-minute conversation with journalist Anne Nivat covered the war in Ukraine, Europe’s future security architecture and Minsk’s relations with the EU, as well as prospects for a possible settlement.
According to BelTA, the Belarusian leader argued that a trilateral meeting between Belarus, Ukraine and Russia would produce results faster than negotiations involving European representatives.
His remarks echoed Moscow’s earlier refusal to include Europe at the negotiating table during the Nov. 10-11 talks in Abu Dhabi – the first trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US since February.
“We would reach an agreement faster than with you [Europeans] on ending this war, on how things should be arranged in the future, and so on. And people would welcome it,” he said, framing the region’s future as a matter for Ukraine, Belarus and Russia alone.
At the same time, BelTA reported that he acknowledged France and other EU member states still have a role to play, particularly as they seek to shape Europe’s post-war security order.
Although Minsk continues to present itself as a neutral party and a possible mediator, Belarus remains among Moscow’s closest allies in the war against Ukraine.
It has allowed Russian forces to use its territory to launch the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Lukashenko himself has openly acknowledged that alignment.
Speaking in Minsk on Oct. 2, during a meeting with delegation heads attending a session of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council, he said Belarus would stand with Russia unconditionally and carry out any decision taken by the Kremlin, even if he personally holds different views on certain aspects of the war.
“In the end, we are ‘co-aggressors’ with him. We have one question, which we sometimes discuss jokingly: who is more of an ‘aggressor’ – me or him?” Lukashenko said at the time.
Kyiv has repeatedly rejected Minsk’s claims of neutrality.
In September, during a side event on Belarus hosted by the EU delegation on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Minsk of directly enabling Moscow’s attacks.
“Belarus is Russia’s accomplice in the war against Ukraine,” Sybiha wrote on X. “Its territory, infrastructure, and resources continue to serve Russia’s war machine.”
The issue has also been raised by the Belarusian opposition.
In June, the United Transitional Cabinet warned Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry that Lukashenko may be preparing to join Russia’s war, pointing to constitutional changes, a rapid military buildup and Minsk’s deepening integration with Moscow’s defense industry as signs that Belarus is moving away from neutrality.
On June 4, Zelensky proposed a face-to-face meeting with Putin in a rare open letter to the Russian leader, calling for peace negotiations on neutral ground.
The Kremlin responded by mocking the proposal, saying that if Zelensky wanted to meet, he should come to Moscow – a position it has maintained since.
During an Oct. 27 telephone call with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Putin again said Zelensky should travel to Moscow for direct talks – a venue Kyiv has consistently rejected, insisting instead on a meeting in a neutral location.
“If Zelensky wants it, let him come to Moscow,” Lukashenko told Le Point , according to excerpts published by the magazine on Tuesday, Nov. 24.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Thanksgiving dinner prices hit an all-time high – and one staple is driving the surge
articles.title_zh: Thanksgiving dinner prices hit an all-time high – and one staple is driving the surge
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Hu reports from Hamilton, New Jersey, on how turkey farmers like Artie DiPaola are raising prices this holiday season due to rising production costs.
Americans are facing higher costs this holiday season amid stubborn inflation and the cost of Thanksgiving festivities has increased from last year, a new analysis finds.
The American Institute for Economic Research (AIER) compiled its 2026 Thanksgiving Cost Index, which showed that prices rose 2.6% over the last year to reach an all-time high.
Prices are now significantly higher than they were before the COVID-19 pandemic, with the Thanksgiving Cost Index now up 32.1% from its 2019 level, as the post-pandemic inflation surge never receded even as the pace of price increases slowed.
"Inflation has moderated considerably since 2021 and 2022, but the cumulative increases in food prices are still a substantial burden on American households," AIER senior director of research Peter C. Earle told FOX Business.
THANKSGIVING TRAVEL TO DIP FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS AS HIGHER COSTS WEIGH ON AMERICANS
Turkey and poultry prices rose at more than double the rate of other components in AIER's Thanksgiving Cost Index, Earle said. (Liz Clayman/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Earle noted that prices for turkey and other poultry jumped 8.4% over the past year, which was more than double the price increase for any other component of AIER's Thanksgiving Cost Index – which will be a notable jump given that turkey is the centerpiece of many Americans' Thanksgiving dinners.
"Renewed avian influenza outbreaks, higher diesel costs, and the unusually concentrated seasonal demand for turkeys have pushed prices sharply higher despite an increase in domestic production," Earle said.
THANKSGIVING SHOPPERS FACE HIGHER TURKEY PRICES AS FAMILY FARMS STRUGGLE WITH RISING COSTS
Thanksgiving food prices rose 2.6% from a year ago in AIER's analysis. (Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images)
Thanksgiving food prices overall were up 2.6% in the past year, whereas the cost of meals at home was up 1.8% and food consumed away from home was up 3.5%.
Bread prices have risen 3.3% in the last year, while prices for frozen vegetables were up 2.6%, and canned fruits like cranberry sauce rose 2.3%.
"Those differences make clear that inflation can vary considerably across narrow categories of consumer spending ," Earle said.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Thanksgiving costs are 32.1% higher than they were in 2019 before the pandemic-era inflation surge, AIER noted. (John Moore/Getty Images)

articles.title_orig: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
articles.title_zh: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
articles.content_orig:
An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's Presiding Officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies.
Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29.
Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.
Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially".
Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down."
A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.
Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".
Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties.
"The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said.
"Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities.
"Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard. "Without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting."
After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced".
"We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said.
At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon . Martin was not among them.
Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?"
"It's been a little bit duller without us in here," she added.
In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".
Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November.
The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.
The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.
Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.
She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".
"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.
"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.
"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.
"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."
The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.
A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.
Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.
A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".
"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.
"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.
"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow ends above 50,000; S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow ends above 50,000; S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap
articles.content_orig:
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures are sliding on Tuesday morning, November 24, 2026, as Wall Street cools off from Monday’s blistering tech rally and shifts its focus back to Federal Reserve rate-hike risks, fresh Iran sanctions, and crucial inflation data due before the Thanksgiving holiday.
Early premarket trading shows losses concentrated heavily in technology and artificial intelligence shares , while the blue-chip Dow is experiencing a more modest pullback ahead of the 9:30 a.m. ET opening bell.
As of roughly 7:04 to 7:33 a.m. ET, all three major U.S. equity index futures were trading in the red:
Tuesday’s dip is largely a breather after one of Wall Street’s most explosive sessions in years. On Monday, November 23, the Dow surged 3.01%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.73%, and the Nasdaq Composite soared 6.51% —marking the biggest single-day gains for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025.
That rally was triggered by Nvidia’s stunning decision to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO , which sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing 31.5% —its best day in 23 years—and restored nearly $1 trillion in market value. Still, a nalysts say Huang’s return does not erase deeper investor jitters over debt-funded AI data center spending , regulatory scrutiny, or Huang’s upcoming congressional testimony on December 3.
"Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "The return of Huang does not mean that the challenges facing AI are over."
Beyond tech profit-taking, macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds are pressuring futures. Traders are now pricing in a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting—along with a 5% chance of a jumbo 50-basis-point increase, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. New York Fed President John Williams reinforced those concerns Monday, stating that persistently high inflation points toward tighter monetary policy.
The rapid whipsaw in AI stocks is also testing Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, with Evercore ISI’s Krishna Guha warning that talk of faster tightening adds stress while Warsh’s silence leaves markets guessing on his stance. The rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.67%.
Geopolitical tensions added another layer of caution after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel, alongside reports of tanker incidents east of the Strait of Hormuz. Even so, energy and metals traded lower early Tuesday, with Brent crude dipping to $88.75 a barrel (near a three-month low), gold easing to $3,619.70 an ounce, and copper giving back 3%.
While steep red numbers in premarket trading can look alarming, strategists emphasize that Tuesday’s pullback is not a market crash—and gives back only a fraction of Monday’s massive gains. Even a 1.5% to 2% dip in Nasdaq futures barely dents the index’s 6.5% surge from the prior session.
Overseas markets also reflected lingering momentum from Monday’s U.S. rebound: Taiwanese shares rallied 9% (with TSMC and Foxconn nearing their 10% daily limits), South Korea’s Kospi jumped roughly 6.3% to 7%, and Japan’s Nikkei climbed nearly 4%, while Europe’s STOXX 600 slipped just 0.1%. Because premarket futures trade on thinner volume overnight, early losses can still narrow—or reverse—once regular U.S. trading begins at 9:30 a.m. ET.

articles.title_orig: Desperate Gamers Are Trying Bring GTA 6 To PCs And Break Free Of Its 30 Fps Cap
articles.title_zh: Desperate Gamers Are Trying Bring GTA 6 To PCs And Break Free Of Its 30 Fps Cap
articles.content_orig:
Let the recompilation efforts begin.
We still don't know when we'll get a true PC port of Grand Theft Auto 6 (rumors point to early next year ), but that's not stopping developers from trying to make unofficial PC ports from happening. Separately, gamers have found a few ways to move beyond the game's 30 fps framerate cap, which makes everything look far more sluggish than modern 60 fps titles like the Ocarina of Time remake .
It's been less than a week since Grand Theft Auto 6 has been released, and it's surprising to see so much progress already being made. When it comes to PC ports, Rockstar has already taken down the Discord server for the Leonida project, which reportedly got GTA 6 to successfully boot up . But Leonida isn't alone. The site "Port Watch VI" is currently tracking several recompilation efforts, and claims to have seen the leading project load the game and allow players to move and talk to NPCs "very slowly."
Even though Rockstar will likely be quick to crack down, we'll likely see more ports spring up now that the hacking group Cyberleek has reportedly dumped files from GTA 6's Xbox build, as well as an executable that could help developers recompile the game.
There's a good chance that an unofficial GTA 6 PC release will arrive before Rockstar's official port. Modern game recompilation efforts are often helped by AI coding tools , and they focus specifically on making games work on PC hardware seamlessly, instead of emulating an entire console.
For people who have GTA 6 on the PS5, modders have already found ways to boost the game's perceived performance through the video enhancement tool Veyra and NVIDIA's DLSS 5, according to Videocardz . Running the PS5 version of the game through a 4K capture card, or via Sony's Remote Play feature , allows Veyra to apply frame generation and other DLSS 5 enhancements to go beyond the game's 30 fps console limit. It's not a perfect solution, though, since both frame generation, GPU enhancements and remote streaming all introduce significantly latency.
For Xbox GTA 6 players, an easy-to-perform glitch unlocks a 40fps version of the game, which should look noticeably smoother than the stock 30 fps. It's unclear how long that glitch will stick around, though, as it really is simple to do. Rockstar has confirmed that we won't be seeing an official 60 fps console mode because their CPUs aren't powerful enough to support simulating such a complex environment at higher frame rates.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Stock Sinks Below IPO Price. What History Says Happens Next.
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Stock Sinks Below IPO Price. What History Says Happens Next.
articles.content_orig:
Shares of Anthropic closed down 6.5% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price.
The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout.
Anthropic's initial public offering was oversubscribed, and roughly half of the institutional investors that placed orders for the stock were left empty-handed, as CNBC previously reported . But at least for now, as the market wavers, those firms don't appear to be racing to scoop up shares.
Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday.
Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending."
Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target.
"The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.
Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market."
"While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme."
Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock.
They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company.
"While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note.

articles.title_orig: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
articles.title_zh: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia . Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.
Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC , the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.
But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill , who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."
Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections , as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.
"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."
Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.
"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.
"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.
Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.
There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."
"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.
Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.
"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin , D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.
"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"
Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.
At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.
"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.
Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.
"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security,"  MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."
Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."
Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk , who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."
But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.
"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.
"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."

articles.title_zh: MU Stock Downgraded, Price Target Cut By Almost $1,000: BNP Paribas Flags 2028 Hyperscaler Capacity Risks
articles.content_orig:
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Micron Technology (MU) shares tracked lower in morning trade on Tuesday after BNP Paribas downgraded the memory-chip maker and cut its price target by more than half, warning that demand risks could emerge in 2028 even as the AI boom drives memory sales.
In a note to investors cited by TheFly, BNP Paribas analyst Karl Ackerman lowered his rating to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Outperform’ and cut his price target to $775 from $1,700. The new target is roughly 54% below his previous estimate, but still implies about 9.5% upside from Monday's close of $707.70.
MU stock fell over 7% in morning trade amid broader market weakness. Shares had surged 19% on Monday, their biggest one-day gain in six months, amid a broader market rebound following Nvidia's (NVDA) reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang .
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Ackerman said risks are building around hyperscalers' capacity plans for 2028, which could threaten the memory industry's supply-demand balance. BNP also pointed to a reduction in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) content in Nvidia's Vera Rubin Ultra platform.
The analyst also expects PC and mobile unit sales to decline in 2026 and 2027, while additional wafer capacity comes online.
More production capacity could increase chip supply at a time when demand growth may be slowing, putting pressure on memory pricing.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
BNP's cautious outlook contrasts with Micron's expectations for continued supply constraints.
In its latest earnings call, Micron said it expects demand to outstrip supply in both 2027 and 2028, and that it still has no clear timeline for when the market will return to balance. The company also said it had secured commitments for the vast majority of its 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply.
Reports about Nvidia adjusting memory specifications for its next-generation AI systems surfaced earlier this year. TrendForce reported in October that Samsung and SK Hynix (SKHY) were preparing lower-spec 8-Hi HBM4 memory for the platform, with production expected in 2027. The reports also suggested Nvidia was reducing memory bandwidth requirements, potentially easing supply constraints.

Nvidia has not publicly confirmed the reported changes, and the reports did not identify Micron as directly affected.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Micron trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, accompanied by chatter at ‘high’ levels.
Micron shares have fallen over 40% from their June peak. BNP’s $775 price target is also far below the roughly $1,593 average target from analysts tracked by Koyfin. Data showed 28 ‘Buy’ ratings, two ‘Hold’ ratings and no ‘Sell’ ratings among 30 analysts covering the stock.

articles.title_orig: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.title_zh: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.content_orig:
The United States is finalizing a new round of tariffs against China, the EU, and a dozen other countries accused by the Department of Commerce of harming U.S. industry by subsidizing their domestic manufacturers, according to The Wall Street Journal . This is the latest move by the Trump administration to fully restore the trade wall that the president erected on April 2 of last year with indiscriminate tariffs on the entire world, but which were overturned by the Supreme Court.
Several U.S. media outlets are expecting U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to announce the results of the tariff investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 this week. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has been analyzing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favor surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms the U.S. industry. Greer’s team is investigating alleged industrial aid from China, the European Union, and 14 other countries.
The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court’s setback . The court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies because it considered that Trump had exceeded his authority by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to approve tariffs, when this law did not authorize him to do so.
After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labor; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. The latter is expected to be approved soon.
The new tariff will be added to the one approved last July , which affected nearly a hundred countries, including EU members, for allegedly violating forced labor import rules. However, it is being challenged in court.
The federal administration has not disclosed how much the new customs duties will amount to, but they will be similar to those Trump set earlier last year. In any case, they will not exceed the levels set in trade agreements and will be applied specifically to each economy, rather than imposed as a general rate, according to Bloomberg.
It is expected that countries and blocs that signed trade agreements with the United States, such as Japan or the EU, will receive special treatment so that the new tariff complies with the agreements. It is therefore anticipated that tariffs will be 15% or less. Other countries, however, would be set higher tariffs.
China could receive a higher tariff, as the Trump Administration has emphasized that its production subsidies are widespread and particularly harmful to the global economy. Moreover, this would counter criticism arising from the Nvidia case that the White House has been too lenient with China.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.content_orig:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU security agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks â what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" â have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much â but not all â of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states â Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania â all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted in August by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Is Falling Again. Why the Jensen Jubilation Is Already Fading.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Falling Again. Why the Jensen Jubilation Is Already Fading.
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_zh: Putin Says Ukraine Hits Russian Oil Plants Despite Trump's Requests, Promises Retaliation
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine continues attacks on Russia n oil refineries despite requests from U.S. President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russia n leader Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday, pledging to retaliate.
Kyiv has said it would stop striking Russia n energy targets only when Moscow did the same and while Ukrainian strikes subsided after Trump's mid-October declaration of energy ceasefire they have picked up again since the end of last month.
"We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the U.S. president's appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice," Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.
"In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable," he said.
He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.
According to estimates from two industry sources, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russia n oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October.
Several Russia n regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of gasoline and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.
Putin said that while the situation on domestic fuel market remained difficult, gasoline prices have stabilized after they peaked in October.
The European Union has decided to completely stop buying Russia n seaborne liquefied natural gas starting from Jan. 1, though Russia n LNG supplies to Europe still reached around 13.7 million metric tons last year.
According to LSEG preliminary data, Russia n LNG exports to Europe increased by around 6.3% year-on-year in the first 10 months of this year, totalling 11.8 million tons.
Putin said that Europe's efforts to curb Russia n energy exports backfired, with Russia expanding its sales markets and increasingly using the Northern Sea Route across its Arctic shores.

CoreWeave stock rose 22.3% on Monday, November 23, 2026. The S&P 500 gained 4.7% the same session. There was no earnings report or SEC filing from the company around the move. The gain came the day Nvidia 's board reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
Investors saw cloud companies that borrowed money to buy Nvidia's chips as among the biggest winners from his return. CoreWeave and Oracle were two of them, and both stocks rose sharply that day.
CoreWeave owed $66.2 billion at the end of September 2026. At Monday's close, that debt was 245.1% of its stock market value. For the S&P 500 as a whole, debt is 20.2% of stock market value.
CoreWeave owes more than twice what its shares are worth, and its stock fell 12% on Friday before Monday's gain. Drops that size are hard to sit through when your savings have to cover the bills. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays .
On its November 10 earnings call, management said it expects to fund most of the remaining capital spending needed to deliver its order backlog with loans tied to specific customer contracts. For more on its borrowing, see Why CoreWeave Can't Pay Down Debt From Its Cash .
CoreWeave rose with its group, but much further. Its sub-industry is systems software. The 29 other companies in it worth $2 billion or more had a median gain of 5.6%. Of those, 28 rose and 1 fell. In all, 18 of them gained five percent or more.
The SPDR technology sector fund, XLK, rose 9%. All five companies on Trefis's peer list for CoreWeave rose: Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , Nvidia and Oracle. Nvidia gained 31.5% and Oracle gained 12.3%. Of the five, only Microsoft is also in the systems software count above.
CoreWeave had 2 rises at least this big in the past year before Monday. The latest was a 24.7% gain on November 11.
Monday's gain followed a 12% fall on Friday, November 20. Friday's close of $39.51 was its lowest close of the past twelve months. For Friday's fall, see What Is Behind The Move In CoreWeave Stock?
The stock is still far below its highest close of the past twelve months, $137.98 on May 6. Counting dividends, it lost 45.1% over the past three months. From the November 20, 2025 close, it lost 30.2%, while the S&P 500 gained 12%.
CoreWeave's stock market value is 2.7 times its sales over the past four quarters, a measure called price to sales. The S&P 500 as a whole trades at 3.1 times its sales.
The next check is CoreWeave's report for the fourth quarter of 2026, the three months to December, expected in February 2027. That report will show how its total debt has moved from $66.2 billion at the end of September 2026.
Our read: Monday's gain came from news at another company, not at CoreWeave. When one stock can swing that hard on someone else's news, it makes sense to spread your money across many strong companies instead of one.

articles.content_orig:

60 Minutes is beset with troubles as it suffered another week of low ratings in the latest blow to CBS News boss Bari Weiss.
CBS News’ flagship newsmagazine has seen ratings tumble ever since Weiss, who took on the role of editor-in-chief in October 2025, began a massive overhaul of the core-three broadcast news network.
60 Minutes drew an average of 8.3 million viewers for the nine episodes that aired from Sept. 9 through Nov. 15, a 16-percent drop from last season, according to preliminary Nielsen data obtained by the Wall Street Journal.
That also includes a nearly 25-percent drop among viewers ages 25 to 54, which is the key demographic for advertisers.
The bad news comes as the show opened its 59th season in September with its smallest premiere audience in at least a quarter century, with just 6.5 million viewers tuning in, according to Nielsen numbers.
The show’s continuous fall in ratings follows a tumultuous year at CBS News, after billionaire David Ellison acquired Paramount — CBS News’ parent company — and appointed Weiss, an “anti-woke” conservative columnist, as editor-in-chief in October last year.
Weiss, who came into the role with no prior broadcast experience, ousted several veteran 60 Minutes correspondents, including Scott Pelley and Cecilia Vega. Another longtime correspondent, Sharyn Alfonsi, left after her contract expired and amid a dispute with Weiss.
Weiss, who founded The Free Press, a conservative-leaning news and opinion site on Substack, later hired former New York Times and Vanity Fair writer Nick Bilton to lead 60 Minutes, though he also had no prior experience in TV news.
Weiss later filled the empty roles with more conservative-leaning hires, including New York Times opinion columnist Ross Douthat and British broadcaster Sir Trevor Philips, who has defended Jeffrey Esptein-tied Lord Peter Mandelson.
Weiss has also been accused by critics of swaying the network’s coverage to be more favorable toward the Trump administration and Israel. However, she has denied those claims.
The network’s struggling news ratings also come as routine discussions over editorial decisions have repeatedly been leaked to the media, fueling speculation over troubles at the show under Weiss and Bilton’s leadership.
Bilton told the Journal that his focus is on the show’s content, not its ratings.
“I can control how good the stories are, the mix of the stories,” he said. “And I truly believe that [if] you continue to do that, you continue to put out great journalism, great storytelling, your audience comes.” Weiss declined to comment to the Journal.
The Independent has contacted CBS News for comment.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.title_zh: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.content_orig:
Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi , as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”
However, on Tuesday, Utah decided to drop the criminal charges against Kalshi, McGavick confirmed to Ars. In a statement on X, Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth said, “We are pleased that Utah has chosen to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi, while proceeding with civil litigation. Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized. We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”
In a press release , Brown explained that the charges were dropped specifically due to the pause.
“Kalshi said it would geofence Utah, which blocks access to its site in the state,” the press release said. “The company also committed to monitor for Utah-based IP addresses trying to reach its site. The Office then reevaluated its position and moved to dismiss the criminal case against the company and the individual defendants.”
Brown threatened that the charges would be raised again if Kalshi tried to renew operations.
“Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Brown said. Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every company in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”
Discussion of the Kalshi pause in a Utah sub-Reddit found some Redditors skeptical of the state’s cases as potentially overreaching.
However, many top commenters seemed pleased with the enforcement efforts, suggesting that Utah may have bipartisan support among some residents. One commenter cheered on the attorney general’s efforts as “the one item in the Utah GOP’s agenda I can get behind,” while another agreed that “prediction markets are incredibly toxic and are manipulated against ordinary people.”
Many complained that Kalshi ads flooded their social media feeds. Some suggested the state should focus on banning advertising of prediction markets, while potentially still allowing adults to trade on event contracts if they want to throw their “money away.”
Fears of insider trading were also raised. One commenter laid out why prediction markets seem suspiciously designed to promote insider trading and other market manipulation:
“I’m pretty libertarian and hate banning things. But gambling and prediction markets are a scourge. Even the term ‘prediction market’ is a misnomer. Because ultimately when people with big dollars get involved it creates a financial incentive for them to make fucked up things happen in the real world. Think about it, decades ago we understood that sports betting was a problem because it corrupted sports—s omething that ultimately is pretty meaningless. Then we got all these people betting on the stock market with puts and it created huge incentives to cause havoc with markets. Now if people are betting big money on politics and wars and everything else, it just means people with influence can make money by making improbable/unexpected things happen.”
One commenter joked, “I wonder how Kashi would have reacted if the judge in charge of their case had ‘traded’ $500,000 on the event of them losing the case. Not a problem at all, right?”
On the same day Kalshi announced its temporary pause in Utah, a judge rejected a request from New York Attorney General Letitia James to immediately shut down Kalshi in that state, Courthouse News reported .
New York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane said she was “uncomfortable” granting the temporary restraining order so early in the case because “there does seem to be an indication that there would be market disruption that I’m concerned about.” Kalshi attorney Grant Mainland described it a little differently, claiming that a sudden halt would cause a “market emergency.”
“I think this is the ultimate relief in the case, which is improper for me to do without full briefing,” Crane said. Instead of granting James’ request, she recommended that Kalshi take steps to address the state’s top concerns by considering “safeguards for users between 18 and 20,” who are under the state’s legal gambling age, Courthouse News reported.
According to Kalshi’s estimates, New York’s Kalshi user base (1.5 million) is much larger than Utah’s, so the market disruption from the Utah shutdown may not have carried the same dire stakes for Kalshi or its broader user base.
The CFTC has sought to intervene in that case, too, and it seems clear that Kalshi expects the questions of who can regulate prediction markets and what trading qualifies as a “bet” to reach the Supreme Court. Kalshi’s spokesperson did not respond to Ars’ questions on how the Utah pause broadly impacted users or the platform.
So far, “three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate prediction markets, while a fourth found they cannot,” Courthouse News reported. But despite the current balance tipping toward allowing states to regulate prediction markets, Kalshi appears confident that the Supreme Court will resolve the disparate court rulings in its favor.
In a lawsuit filed by a disgruntled Kalshi user, Kalshi argued that it would waste lower courts’ time to continue litigating these cases and that no case should be resolved until the Supreme Court weighs in.
In that case, Kalshi user Scott Bright alleged that he lost more than $300,000 on sports bets that were technically illegal in Washington.
According to Kalshi, all of Bright’s claims rest “on the premise that state gambling laws reach KalshiEX’s federally regulated exchange—the question now before the Supreme Court. Plaintiff puts the cart before the horse; Defendants ask only that the Court let that threshold question be resolved first.”
The court has yet to address Kalshi’s request to stay the case, but Bright has argued that Kalshi is trying to “sideline a case governed by binding Ninth Circuit precedent so that they can wait for a Supreme Court decision that may never come.”

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.
